about: Lessons for the ledger example. Each is one a capable agent wouldn't get right from the error, the docs or unprompted, checked against the docs on 27 October 2026 (the last three on 2 November 2026). `theirs`: what other people's agents learned using the ideas the change rests on, each with what came of it for other projects, seeded into the stand-in graph in this order, each with the card the real graph would make for it from its words: what it's matched by; `contradicts` names an earlier one by its place in this list, from 0: another good way, linked both ways. `story`: what the example's agent meets as it works on the change, as Claude Code's hook gives it to `kelve moment`: files it reads and edits, the usual way written where another agent found a better one, a test that fails with an error that points the wrong way and then passes, and work of its own it replaces with a better way. `learned`: what it writes, when kelve asks.

theirs.says: A unique violation as a charge's key is stored after the charge means a second try got past the lookup and was charged too. Storing the key with `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` makes the error go away and leaves the double charge. `SELECT … FOR UPDATE` on the lookup doesn't stop it: it locks only rows already there.
theirs.do: Claim the key with an insert before charging, and charge only when your insert made the row.
theirs.example:
INSERT INTO requests (key) VALUES ($1)
  ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING
  RETURNING key  -- no row: another try has it
theirs.holdsWhen: Postgres at read committed, its default, when tries of one request can arrive together.

variants: error returned from database: duplicate key value violates unique constraint <str>
ERROR:  duplicate key value violates unique constraint <str>

theirs.seenAs: error returned from database: duplicate key value violates unique constraint <str>

theirs.says: `ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING RETURNING` gives no row when the key is already there, so a retry needs a second query for the first try's row. A no-op update, `DO UPDATE SET key = excluded.key`, returns the stored row in the same statement, at the cost of writing it again.
theirs.do: Get the stored row back in the same statement, with `ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET key = excluded.key RETURNING`.
theirs.example:
INSERT INTO requests (key) VALUES ($1)
  ON CONFLICT (key) DO UPDATE SET key = excluded.key
  RETURNING receipt
theirs.holdsWhen: Postgres 9.5 and later, where writing the row again, and an update trigger firing, on a retry don't matter.

theirs.says: When `ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING RETURNING` gives no row, a `SELECT` of the key in a second statement finds the stored row, even one another transaction was still writing: the insert waits for that transaction, and at read committed the next statement sees what it committed. Nothing is written again on a retry.
theirs.do: When `DO NOTHING RETURNING` gives no row, select the stored row in a second statement.
theirs.holdsWhen: Postgres at read committed, its default, where writing the row on every retry would cost more than a second query.

theirs.says: Jitter from a generator seeded the same way in every copy of a client gives every copy the same waits, so copies that failed together still retry together. Seeding from the clock in seconds does it to copies started in the same second. Go's `math/rand` did it by default before Go 1.20, starting every process from the same seed unless it was seeded.
theirs.do: Draw jitter from a generator the operating system seeds, such as Rust's `rand::thread_rng()` or Go's top-level `math/rand` from 1.20, never one seeded from the clock.
theirs.example:
// Rust: seeded from the OS, separately in every process and thread
let wait = rand::thread_rng().gen_range(Duration::ZERO..=ceiling);
theirs.holdsWhen: Many copies of one client, deployed or restarted together, each picking its own jitter.

theirs.says: `base * 2u32.pow(attempt)` overflows on the 33rd try, before `.min(ceiling)` can cap it. A debug build panics with `attempt to multiply with overflow`; a release build wraps the power to 0, so the wait drops to nothing and the client retries in a tight loop against the service it was backing off from.
theirs.do: Keep the power from overflowing before the ceiling applies: cap the exponent, or use `saturating_pow` and `saturating_mul`.
theirs.holdsWhen: Rust, a retry loop with no limit on tries, or one past 32, that works out each wait as a power of two.

variants:
thread <str> panicked at <str>:
attempt to multiply with overflow

theirs.says: A serialization failure (40001) or a deadlock (40P01) in Postgres passes if tried again, but only as the whole transaction. After any error in a transaction, every later statement fails with `current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block`, so retrying just the statement that failed never works.
theirs.do: On 40001 or 40P01, roll back and run the whole transaction again from its first statement, with the retry loop around the transaction.
theirs.holdsWhen: Postgres, at repeatable read or serializable, or wherever two transactions lock the same rows in different orders.
theirs.seenAs: current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block

variants: ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of transaction block

tool_input.new_string: sqlx::query("INSERT INTO requests (key, receipt) VALUES ($1, $2) ON CONFLICT (key) DO NOTHING")

lessons.says: One timeout around a whole retry loop lets a slow first try use up all the time, so the retries it was there for never run. A timeout on each try ends the slow one and leaves time for the next; a deadline around the loop can still cap the whole.
lessons.do: Give each try its own timeout inside the retry loop, as well as any deadline around it.
lessons.holdsWhen: Any retry loop around a call that can hang, such as a request to another service.
